courses.name: Introduction to Computing I
courses.blurb: My first programming course in a classroom.

comments.title: Learning from someone else
comments.text:
The prof was great. I always think the professor you have for that first relevant course dictates how much you'll like, and how well you'll perform in, the classes that build on it.

This was my first introduction to programming in a classroom. Before that, I was self-taught in anything tech related, but I realized there's a lot other people can teach you that you can't necessarily teach yourself. That really stuck with me, and it's motivated me to pay attention in class to this day.

courses.name: Technical Report Writing
courses.blurb: Writing precisely and clearly, ending in a technical report.

comments.title: Precise and clear
comments.text:
I had to write a technical report, but overall the class taught me the importance of being precise and clear in my explanations, even in domains that may be considered informal.

To this day, because of this class, I can spot every grammar mistake.

courses.name: Spanish
courses.blurb: Grammar, verb conjugation and vocabulary, with a dose of culture.

comments.title: A reintroduction to a language I love
comments.text:
I liked this course because it was a reintroduction to proper grammar and overall knowledge of the language.

I had my first Spanish class when I was 9, and ever since, I've loved the culture, including the language.

courses.name: Introduction to Calculus and Vectors
courses.blurb: Ontario grade 12 math, sped up: functions, limits, derivatives and vectors.

comments.title: My first uni term
comments.text:
Since I decided to skip CEGEP and go directly to university, I had to take this as a makeup class. It's essentially a sped-up course on what you would learn in grade 12 math in Ontario.

I liked this course, but it stressed me out because it was my first university term. I was so proud when I did well in it.

documents.title: Calculus and vectors notes
documents.note: 6 pages, including midterm and final exam summary sheets (22 MB).

courses.name: Introduction to Psychology
courses.blurb: Human behaviour, the nervous system, and how psychology runs experiments.

comments.title: Psychology is a science
comments.text:
I've always had an interest in human behaviour, and this class gave me a more scientific approach to it. I got to see how different chemicals and drugs affect our nervous system and our behaviour, and which parts of our body let us do different things. Very fascinating stuff overall.

I can't post the notes here because it's not authorized, but I hope this comment makes you a bit more interested in psychology, **which is indeed a science**, by the way.

Fun fact: did you know anything that follows the scientific method is a science? I learned that in this course, since it also covered how to design different types of experiments in psychology for a specific desired outcome.

courses.docsNote: The course notes aren't authorized for sharing, so there are none here.

courses.name: Introduction to Computing II
courses.blurb: Object-oriented programming in a statically typed language, and building your own data types.

comments.title: Static vs. dynamic
comments.text:
I disliked this course for reasons I won't mention. I will say, though, that it was interesting to be able to make your own data types and use them in different ways.

As much as I don't like statically typed languages, they are useful, and in my opinion it's easier to "customize" your own stuff with them. It's a compromise I always have to make between static and dynamic languages, but both have their benefits.

courses.name: Calculus I
courses.blurb: Limits, derivatives and integrals, and all the problems they let you solve.

comments.title: Solving problems in unexpected ways
comments.text:
The winter is brutal, so I was extra unmotivated to go above and beyond. I had a difficult start, but I ended up performing well in it by the end.

What I liked about calculus is how it introduces you to solving all kinds of problems in ways you wouldn't necessarily expect.

I also liked that the professor had a sense of humour and clearly loved teaching the course. It motivated me to attend classes and take it seriously during an unmotivating time, and he had faith in me to succeed and do very well, which is what ended up happening by the end.

courses.name: Discrete Mathematics for Computing
courses.blurb: Logic, sets, proofs, counting, recurrences and graphs: the math underneath computer science.

comments.title: So many different topics
comments.text:
The winter is brutal, so I was extra unmotivated to go above and beyond. I had a difficult start, but I ended up performing well in it by the end.

What I loved about discrete math is how diverse the topics are. There are so many different things in it, and that's what makes it so interesting.

courses.name: Digital Systems I
courses.blurb: How computers work at the lowest level: binary, Boolean algebra, logic gates, combinational and sequential circuits.

comments.title: Why I loved it
comments.text: What I loved about this course was learning how computers work at the lowest level. It was insightful, and it was the beginning of me seeing how everything pieces together when it comes to computers overall.

courses.name: Discrete Structures
courses.blurb: Discrete math, continued: deeper topics with a programming layer, including encryption.

comments.title: Alice and Bob hurt me a little
comments.text:
This class is a continuation of discrete math that goes into more in-depth topics, and I like that it has a programming layer to it.

In my course sequence I was technically supposed to take it later, but I chose to take it during the summer, and it ended up helping me a lot in one of my other courses.

Just like discrete math, I like the diversity of topics. Encryption and decryption was one of my favourite parts, but even so, Alice and Bob did hurt me a little, lol (if you know, you know).

courses.name: Introduction to Linear Algebra
courses.blurb: Vectors, lines and planes, subspaces, span, matrices: the language of optimization.

comments.title: The math behind optimization
comments.text:
What I liked is how crucial linear algebra is to optimization systems. It really put into perspective how things can genuinely be specified.

I spent my whole high school career optimizing individual functions one by one because I was so unaware, but now it's very good to know, lol.

courses.name: Calculus II
courses.blurb: Integration techniques and applications, sequences and series: a little theory, mostly applications.

comments.title: From scary to a favourite
comments.text:
This class scared me so much. I'd heard nightmare stories about it, I knew a lot of people ended up having to retake it, and I was scared I'd be the worst at it.

It ended up being one of my favourite courses. I liked how the material has some theory, but it's mostly applications. Overall, I like seeing how my courses apply in real life. It's something I value a lot when I'm learning literally anything. Sure, not everything needs to be super important, but if I invest a lot of time into something, I like seeing how it can benefit me.

Also, the prof I had was super chill, and I loved it.
